w: The King's working palace began as the citadel of Fes el-Jdid, founded in 1276 by the Marinids. Most of what stands today dates from the Alawi centuries after. The public only sees its edges: the Old Mechouar gate to the northeast, and the brass-studded 20th-century doors at Place des Alaouites, near the Mellah, still guarded.

s: Fes el-Jdid's oldest mosque, with a tomb maybe fit for a sultan
q: Great Mosque of Fes el-Jdid fes
w: Fes el-Jdid's founding mosque went up in 1276, the same year the Marinids carved this royal citadel out of the hills west of old Fez, making it the district's oldest mosque. Behind its hypostyle hall and ornate minaret sits a mausoleum with several tombs; one is popularly said to hold Sultan Abu Inan, though no inscription confirms it.

s: The 'Red Mosque' anchoring Fes el-Jdid's main street
w: Everyone calls it the Red Mosque, though its proper name is al-Hamra. The Marinids built it as a neighbourhood Friday mosque for Fes el-Jdid, right along what's now the Grande Rue, the royal citadel's main street, still lined with the ordinary shops and comings and goings the mosque was built to serve.

s: A 20th-century relic of Fez's indigenous Jewish rite
w: Reputed to be one of the oldest synagogues in Fez, Slat al-Fassiyine held onto something rare well into the 20th century: the rituals of the toshavim, Morocco's indigenous Jews, rather than the Sephardic rite that came to dominate elsewhere. Neglect closed it in 1970; a careful restoration reopened its doors in 2013.

s: The northwestern gate into the old walled city
w: Bab Guissa is the main gate through the northwestern stretch of Fes el Bali's walls, one of the working entrances that has funnelled traffic, goods and pilgrims into the old medina for centuries, named for the quarter it opens onto and still doing the job today, right down to the mosque and madrasa built into it.

s: 'The Great Climb' — Fes el-Bali's spine of souks and monuments
w: Its name means 'the Great Slope,' and Tala'a Kebira earns it, running the length of Fes el-Bali from the Bab Bou Jeloud and Bab Mahrouk gates in the west to the al-Attarine Madrasa and Qarawiyyin Mosque in the east. It's one of the medina's principal souq streets, and the monuments along the way read like a history of the city.

s: 'Mosque of Stone,' raised by Sultan Abu Inan in 1357
w: Its formal name translates roughly as 'Mosque of the Lady of the Orange Tree's Flower,' but locals call it Jama' el-Hajjar, the Mosque of Stone, after its carved stone portal. The Marinid sultan Abu Inan completed it in 1357 in Fes el-Jdid, and the nickname has long outlasted the official one.

s: 'Gate of order' into the Marinids' royal city
w: Bab al-Amer means 'gate of order,' and it was the southwestern entrance to Fes el-Jdid, the fortified royal city the Marinids founded in 1276 just west of old Fez. It's one of a handful of monumental gates that still mark the edges of a citadel built, from the outset, to keep the sultan's court apart from the city proper.

s: Fez's very first mosque, now just a fragment of itself
w: This was Fez's original mosque, raised by Idris I in the early 9th century at the same moment he founded the city, older than the Qarawiyyin, older than everything. Known first as the Mosque of the Lights, then the Mosque of the Chiefs, it was eclipsed by the nearby Mosque of the Andalusians. Only fragments of it remain today.

s: Marinid garden gate whose towers still stand
w: Built in 1286 as an entrance to the Marinid royal gardens north of Fes el-Jdid, Bab Segma has long since stopped functioning as a working gate, but its twin towers are still standing, and the name has stuck around as a toponym for the neighbourhood even after the gardens it once guarded disappeared entirely.

s: A medieval mosque and madrasa tucked beside Bab Guissa
w: Standing right beside the gate that shares its name, the Bab Guissa Mosque is one of the medina's medieval Friday mosques, with an adjoining madrasa still attached, a reminder that Fez's gates were rarely just gates, but whole religious and civic complexes folded into the city walls.

s: A sultan's mosque doubling as the Alawi dynasty's tomb
w: Moulay Abdallah ruled Morocco on and off between 1729 and 1757, and this mosque he founded in Fes el-Jdid is also where he ended up, buried in the necropolis attached to it, alongside later generations of the Alawi dynasty. It's a rare combination in the old royal city: a working mosque that doubles as a royal burial ground.

s: Where the 1912 Treaty of Fes was signed away
w: Beneath the lavish stucco and cedar of this early 20th-century palace on Tala'a Seghira, Morocco's independence was quietly signed away: the 1912 Treaty of Fes, which handed the country to French rule as a protectorate, was formalised inside these walls. The architecture alone would make it worth a stop; the history makes it essential.
